title: Verb second & inversion
rule: A Dutch statement starts with one whole constituent, then the finite verb. If time or place comes first, the subject follows the verb.

title: Omdat · explain a reason
rule: Omdat introduces a reason in a subordinate clause. Its finite verb comes after the other clause elements. Practise one verb first; longer verb groups have additional rules.
example: Ik werk thuis omdat de trein niet rijdt.

title: Dat · say what you think
rule: Dat means that here and introduces the content of a thought, statement or message. The subordinate clause has its verb toward the end. This is different from demonstrative dat.
example: Ik denk dat de server werkt.

title: Als · conditions & repeated situations
rule: Als can mean if, or when for a recurring situation. If the als clause comes first, the main clause begins with its finite verb followed by its subject.
example: Als ik hulp nodig heb, bel ik mijn collega.

title: Tot · until something happens
rule: Tot introduces the endpoint of an action. In a tot clause the subject comes before its objects and the finite verb comes at the end in these examples.
example: Ik wacht tot de dokter me roept.

title: Toen · one past occasion
rule: Use toen for when on a particular occasion in the past. The toen clause uses subordinate order. When it comes first, the following main clause begins with verb then subject.
example: Toen ik thuiskwam, belde ik Zoë.

title: Verbs in context
rule: Use a finite verb that matches the subject and tense. With a perfect auxiliary, the action uses a participle. Being is not added before an already conjugated action verb.
example: Wij proberen het. Wij hebben het geprobeerd.

title: Separable verbs
rule: A separable particle moves away from a finite main verb, stays attached in an infinitive after a modal, and surrounds ge- in many participles. Te goes between particle and infinitive.
example: Ik stuur het op. Ik kan het opsturen. Ik heb het opgestuurd.

title: Present, past & perfect
rule: Choose the tense for the situation. Simple past is common in a narrative; perfect often reports what happened. Learn each participle and its auxiliary. Similar events can have different focuses.
example: Ik ga naar de markt. Ik ging naar de markt. Ik ben naar de markt gegaan.
